tasks.task: In the Hugging Face documentation, find the tutorial on loading adapters with PEFT, tell me how to load in 8bit or 4bit.
tasks.answer: To load a PEFT adapter in 8bit or 4bit, you quantize the base model with the bitsandbytes integration via transformers' BitsAndBytesConfig and pass it as quantization_config when loading the model, then attach the adapter with PEFT. 4-bit: from transformers import BitsAndBytesConfig; config = BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_4bit=True, bnb_4bit_quant_type='nf4', bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True, bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16); model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, quantization_config=config, device_map='auto'); model = prepare_model_for_kbit_training(model); then apply LoraConfig/get_peft_model or load the adapter with PeftModel.from_pretrained(model, adapter_id). 8-bit: set load_in_8bit=True in BitsAndBytesConfig instead and pass it the same way as quantization_config. Source: Hugging Face PEFT docs, Developer guides > Quantization (https://huggingface.co/docs/peft/developer_guides/quantization).

Summary of its intro/overview ('What is Waypoint-1.5?'): Waypoint-1.5 is Overworld's next real-time video world model - a diffusion-based generative model that creates interactive, playable worlds on hardware people actually own. Building on the first Waypoint release, which proved real-time generative worlds were possible, version 1.5 improves visual fidelity and broadens hardware support: it generates real-time environments at up to 720p and 60 FPS on RTX 3090-5090 desktops, and adds a new 360p tier for gaming laptops and (soon) Apple Silicon Macs. It was trained on nearly 100x more data than Waypoint-1 and uses more efficient video-modeling techniques, yielding more coherent environments and more consistent motion over time. The overall goal is interactive world simulation without datacenter-scale compute, moving beyond passive video demos toward responsive, explorable worlds people can actually step into.

tasks.task: Investigate the 'transformers' library in the Hugging Face documentation, focusing on how to add new tokens to a tokenizer.
tasks.answer: Investigated the Hugging Face transformers documentation on adding new tokens to a tokenizer. Navigated to the transformers docs index (https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/index) and the Tokenizer API reference (https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main_classes/tokenizer). Key findings: (1) tokenizer.add_tokens(new_tokens, special_tokens=False) adds new regular tokens to the vocabulary — tokens are only added if not already present; accepts str, tokenizers.AddedToken, or a list, and returns the number of tokens added; (2) tokenizer.add_special_tokens(new_tokens) adds special tokens (e.g., extra [CLS]/[SEP]-style tokens); (3) AddedToken wraps a string token to customize its behavior (single-word matching, whitespace stripping, etc.); (4) after adding tokens, call model.resize_token_embeddings(len(tokenizer)) so the model's embedding matrix matches the enlarged vocabulary.

tasks.task: Investigate in the Hugging Face documentation how to utilize the 'Trainer' API for training a model on a custom dataset, and note the configurable parameters of the Trainer class.
tasks.answer: Final Response: Investigated the Hugging Face documentation on using the Trainer API for training a model on a custom dataset. Sources: https://huggingface.co/docs (Docs hub), https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/training (Fine-tuning tutorial), and https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main_classes/trainer (Trainer API reference). How to use the Trainer API on a custom dataset: (1) load and tokenize your custom dataset (e.g., with datasets.load_dataset and a tokenizer) to produce input_ids/attention_mask labels; (2) load a pretrained model via AutoModelFor...; (3) configure training hyperparameters with TrainingArguments; (4) instantiate Trainer(model=model, args=training_args, train_dataset=..., eval_dataset=..., processing_class=tokenizer, data_collator=...); (5) call trainer.train() to fine-tune and optionally trainer.push_to_hub() to upload. Key configurable Trainer/TrainingArguments parameters noted from the docs: output_dir, num_train_epochs, per_device_train_batch_size, per_device_eval_batch_size, gradient_accumulation_steps, learning_rate, weight_decay, warmup_steps, logging_steps, eval_strategy, save_strategy, save_steps, fp16, bf16, load_best_model_at_end, metric_for_best_model, report_to, push_to_hub, dataloader_num_workers, optim (plus many more TrainingArguments such as max_steps, lr_scheduler_type, max_grad_norm, seed, evaluation_strategy, logging_dir, resume_from_checkpoint, etc.).
